vignette: A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m2) fell at home 6 hours ago and now has new dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. She is alert, GCS 15, without focal deficits. Heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg, SpO2 90% on room air. Non-contrast CT head shows a 6-mm acute left frontal subdural hematoma without midline shift. CT pulmonary angiography shows bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli with an RV/LV ratio of 1.1. Troponin is mildly elevated. Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, platelets 190,000/mm3.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue apixaban at the current dose
Hold apixaban, give andexanet alfa, and place an inferior vena cava filter
Start a weight-based unfractionated heparin infusion without bolus
Switch apixaban to warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3

imaging: Non-contrast CT head: 6-mm acute left frontal subdural hematoma, no midline shift
CT pulmonary angiography: bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli, RV/LV ratio 1.1

vignette: A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks of gestation presents with 1 day of pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. She has mild swelling of the left calf. Heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, SpO2 95% on room air. Chest radiograph is normal. D-dimer is elevated. She takes prenatal vitamins only. Creatinine is 0.6 mg/dL.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start low-molecular-weight heparin and obtain compression ultrasonography of the left leg
Reassure and discharge because D-dimer is physiologically elevated in pregnancy

vignette: A 81-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m2), atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation, and heart failure presents with 5 hours of severe periumbilical abdominal pain out of proportion to a soft, mildly tender abdomen. Lactate is 4.1 mmol/L. Heart rate 118/min irregular, blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg. Plain abdominal radiograph is unremarkable. He takes furosemide and metoprolol.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: CT angiography of the abdomen now, with intravenous fluids
Non-contrast CT of the abdomen to avoid contrast nephropathy
Abdominal ultrasound and serial lactate in 6 hours
